LESSON: RHYTHM

Grade: Grade 4
Subject: CREATIVE ARTS
Strand: Creating and Executing
Topic 1.4: Rhythm

SECTION 1: WELCOME

Hello! This is a study lesson on Rhythm. Read the explanation, follow every worked example, then do the practice. This is original CBC Learn content written from KICD outcomes — not a copy of a commercial textbook.

Big question: How can a rhythm be created?

SECTION 2: WHAT YOU WILL LEARN

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

1. write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering
2. describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern
3. compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests

SECTION 3: STUDY NOTES (READ AND LEARN)

WHAT YOU ARE STUDYING: RHYTHM
Subject: CREATIVE ARTS · Grade: Grade 4
This is a learner study lesson (not a teacher guide). Read every part, follow the models, then practise.

BIG PICTURE
Rhythm helps you succeed in CREATIVE ARTS. You will understand it, practise it, and use it at home, at your place of worship, and at school.

KEY FACTS: RHYTHM
Study Rhythm like a learner textbook page: meaning → examples → practice → check.
Replace teacher words with your own words.
If a step is unclear, rewrite it shorter and try again.

PART 1: Write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering

What this means
In this part you learn to write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering. You will use ideas from at home, at your place of worship, and at school.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering.
2. Reflect, retell, then practise a good habit using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Value in action: Show how “Rhythm” looks when you treat a classmate kindly.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 2: Describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern

What this means
In this part you learn to describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern. You will use ideas from at home, at your place of worship, and at school.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern.
2. Reflect, retell, then practise a good habit using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Story link: Retell a short faith/values story connected to Rhythm in your own words.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern. Write or say your answer clearly.

PART 3: Compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests

What this means
In this part you learn to compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests. You will use ideas from at home, at your place of worship, and at school.

How to learn it
1. Read the idea carefully: compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests.
2. Reflect, retell, then practise a good habit using a Kenyan example from your life.
3. Check yourself: Can you explain it without looking?

Model
Daily habit: Choose one good action to practise today because of this lesson.

Your turn
Do one short practice that proves you can compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests. Write or say your answer clearly.

PUT IT TOGETHER
Close your notes and say aloud: what Rhythm is, one example, and one way you will practise this week.

SECTION 4: QUICK EXAMPLES

Example 1: Show how “Rhythm” looks when you treat a classmate kindly. (skill: write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering)

Example 2: Retell a short faith/values story connected to Rhythm in your own words. (skill: describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern)

Example 3: Choose one good action to practise today because of this lesson. (skill: compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests)

SECTION 5: PRACTICE NOW

1. Write 5 sentences (or show 5 clear steps) that teach Rhythm to a classmate.
2. Practise this skill: write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering.
3. Practise this skill: describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern.
4. Practise this skill: compose a rhythmic pattern involving a crochet, a pair of quavers and their rests.
5. Make one local Kenya example of Rhythm from your county, market, farm, or school.
6. Mark your own work: What did you get right? What will you redo?

SECTION 6: WORK TO DO (HOME / REVISION)

1. In your exercise book, make a one-page revision sheet for Rhythm: meaning, 3 examples, 5 practice items.
2. Teach a parent/guardian or younger sibling one part of this lesson (2 minutes).
3. Answer in writing: Why should a Grade 4 learner study Rhythm?
4. Prepare for the quiz: cover the Remember box and recite it.

SECTION: THINK ABOUT IT

1. How can a rhythm be created?

SECTION: REMEMBER

1. Know what Rhythm means in your own words.
2. Use local Kenyan examples, not only definitions.
3. Practise in small steps, then check your work.
4. Be able to: write the French rhythm taa and ta-te, names using free hand lettering.
5. Be able to: describe the qualities of a good rhythmic pattern.

Now complete the Revision Quiz. Open Answers only after you finish.

— CBC Learn · Original study notes from KICD outcomes (Strategy 2)
